opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the "white-box" label, because it's not quite how we think about it, even though I understand why people describe it that way.

Glaze takes advantage of the fact that so much of the generative AI ecosystem is built on shared open components. When someone fine-tunes a model to mimic an artist, they're almost always starting from a publicly available base model, and those models rely on feature extractors that encode images into the representation space where the model learns. We have access to those same encoders. So in that sense, yes, we can see inside the parts that matter, and we use that to compute small perturbations to an artist's image. To a human, the art looks essentially the same. In feature space, the image gets pushed toward a different style. When a mimic trains on Glazed images, the model learns the wrong association. It thinks it's learning that artist's style, but what it actually picks up is shifted somewhere else.

But I don't think of it as an attack on a specific model the way the adversarial ML literature often frames white-box attacks. We aren't targeting one fixed classifier and trying to flip its output. We're targeting a whole family of downstream fine-tuning workflows that share common representations. The goal is transferability. The protection has to hold up when someone uses a different checkpoint, a different fine-tuning method like LoRA or DreamBooth, or applies some preprocessing.

There's also an asymmetry I think is important. In the classic security framing, the attacker is the one perturbing inputs and the model owner is the defender. Here it's flipped. The artist is defending their own work, and the person doing mimicry is the one who wants to use that work without consent. So Glaze is a defensive tool that uses adversarial techniques, not an attack in the normal sense.

And we're very clear-eyed about the limits. This is an arms race. Models change, encoders change, people develop countermeasures. Glaze isn't a permanent guarantee. What it does is raise the cost of mimicry and give artists some agency at a point when they have almost none. Our view has always been that technical tools like this buy time while the larger questions around consent, compensation, and regulation get worked out.

r001.rationale: It says the mimic learns from Glazed images during training and acquires a wrong style association, identifying a training-time poisoning effect rather than an inference-time attack.

r002.rationale: It links artist-mimicking models’ use of fine-tuning to publicly available base models, but does not name Stable Diffusion or attribute its prevalence to users’ ability to fine-tune it.

r003.rationale: It says Glaze uses the same encoders as the models’ feature extractors and that downstream workflows share representations, explaining transfer through shared underlying components.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think "white-box" is actually a slightly misleading way to frame it, and it's worth unpacking why. In the classic adversarial ML sense, white-box means you have the exact weights of the model you're attacking, and you compute gradients against that model. Glaze doesn't have that. We don't know what Stable Diffusion checkpoint or what fine-tuning recipe someone is going to use six months from now to mimic a particular artist. We can't know that.

What we do have is access to a feature extractor, the image encoder, that is shared across a lot of these generative models. So the bet Glaze makes is that mimicry works by pulling an artist's style into the model's feature space, and if we can perturb the images so that in that feature space they look like a different style, while to a human they look basically unchanged, then whatever model trains on those images learns the wrong thing. It's an attack on the training pipeline, not on a deployed model. That's the key distinction. We're not fooling a classifier at inference time; we're poisoning what a downstream fine-tuner learns.

So in that sense it's more of a gray-box or transfer setting. We optimize against one encoder and we're relying on transferability to models we never see. And honestly that transferability is the thing that surprised us most. It worked better than I expected, and part of that is that these models share a lot of architectural DNA and a lot of training data.

The other thing I'd say about the "attack" framing is that it's inverted from how the security community usually thinks. Normally the model is the asset and the adversary is the one perturbing inputs. Here the artist is the one being attacked, by people scraping their work and fine-tuning on it without consent, and Glaze is the defense. It just happens to use the machinery of adversarial examples to do it. So I resist calling it an attack on models. The models are the ones doing the taking. We're giving the people who have no other leverage a technical tool that raises the cost of mimicry.

And I want to be honest about the limits. It's not a cryptographic guarantee. It's an arms race. People have published things that partially purify Glaze perturbations, and we've pushed back, and that'll keep going. The goal was never to make mimicry impossible forever. It was to buy artists time and to make it not free, so that the economic and legal conversation could catch up to the technology.

r001.rationale: It says Glaze attacks the training pipeline by poisoning what a downstream fine-tuner learns, rather than fooling a model at inference time.

r002.rationale: It mentions Stable Diffusion checkpoints and fine-tuning, but does not attribute Stable Diffusion’s prevalence to users’ ability to fine-tune it themselves.

r003.rationale: It explains transfer through a shared encoder, architectural similarities, and training data, but does not say the target models use essentially the same underlying model used to generate Glaze.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that we assume the people training these models know what we’re doing. We’re not relying on keeping Glaze a secret. They can understand the algorithm, look at the paper, and potentially try to undo the protection. That’s the white-box threat model, and it’s a much harder setting than assuming an adversary never figures out how your system works.

The intuition behind Glaze is to create a mismatch between what a person sees and what a model learns. An artist can put a piece online that still looks like their work to you and me, but the small changes we make cause the model to interpret its stylistic features differently. If someone then uses those images to fine-tune a model to mimic that artist, the goal is for it to learn the wrong style.

The important question is what happens when that person actively tries to remove those changes. Can they defeat the protection while preserving the stylistic information they wanted to take in the first place? That’s the tension we’re trying to exploit. I wouldn’t describe it as an absolute guarantee. It’s a defensive tool that tries to give artists some leverage in a situation where they otherwise have very little control.

r001.rationale: It describes altered images being used to fine-tune a model so the model learns the wrong style, communicating a poisoning attack during training rather than an inference-time attack.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute Stable Diffusion’s prevalence to users being able to fine-tune it themselves.

r003.rationale: It does not explain Glaze’s transfer by saying artist-mimicking models use essentially the same underlying model as Glaze.

sol-6.1.text:
The way we think about Glaze is as a targeted poisoning attack. The artist wants to share their work, but they don’t want someone to take those images and train a model that mimics their style. So we make very small changes to the image that are difficult for a person to notice, but that change how the model interprets its style. Visually, it’s still your artwork. To the model, the style features point somewhere else.

Now, the white-box part needs a little qualification. We can use an accessible model to compute those changes, but we generally don’t know which model someone will ultimately use to train on the artwork. So we need the protection to transfer across models. Having access to one model gives us a way to construct the perturbation; it doesn’t mean we have access to the eventual mimicry model.

The goal is that, when someone trains on those protected images, they learn the wrong association between the artist and the style. We’re trying to give artists a technical way to push back on that imitation while still being able to show their work.

r001.rationale: The response calls Glaze a targeted poisoning attack and describes changing what models learn during training, distinguishing it from an inference-time attack.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Stable Diffusion or attribute its prevalence to users being able to fine-tune it themselves.

r003.rationale: It says the perturbation should transfer across models but does not explain that transfer by saying artist-mimicking models use essentially the same underlying model used to generate Glaze.
